title: Build Tools (Maven & Gradle)
description: Builds for real projects: modules, version management, plugins, profiles, private repositories and speed.
resumo: Multi-module: a `pom` parent lists modules; the reactor orders them; `-pl x -am` builds one module and its needs. No cycles.
`dependencyManagement` sets versions, `dependencies` adds to the classpath; import BOMs with `type pom` + `scope import`.
Plugins do the work; bind goals to phases with `executions`; pin every version; `help:effective-pom` explains the build.
Maven profiles change how you build, never what each environment gets — one artifact, configured at runtime.
`settings.xml`: mirrors and credentials from environment variables — never passwords in the pom.
Faster builds: build what changed, `-T 1C`, skip unnecessary `clean`, cache `~/.m2` in CI.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the API, a batch job and a shared domain library live in the same repository and must be built and versioned together.

**Concept:** a multi-module project has a parent `pom.xml` with `packaging` `pom` that lists `modules`; each module has its own `pom.xml` that inherits from the parent. Maven's reactor works out the order from the dependencies between modules and builds them in that order. `-pl` selects modules and `-am` ("also make") builds what they depend on.

**How it works:** modules depend on each other like any dependency, usually with `${project.version}`.
examples.code:
shop/
├── pom.xml              # parent: <packaging>pom</packaging>
├── shop-domain/pom.xml
├── shop-api/pom.xml     # depends on shop-domain
└── shop-batch/pom.xml   # depends on shop-domain

<!-- parent pom.xml -->
<modules>
  <module>shop-domain</module>
  <module>shop-api</module>
  <module>shop-batch</module>
</modules>

$ ./mvnw verify                          # everything, in dependency order
$ ./mvnw verify -pl shop-api -am         # shop-api and what it needs
examples.interview_question: How does Maven decide the build order of modules in a multi-module project?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Two modules that depend on each other. Maven cannot choose an order and refuses to build. Move the shared code into a third module both depend on.
examples.code:
[ERROR] The projects in the reactor contain a cyclic reference:
        Edge between 'shop-api' and 'shop-domain' introduces a cycle

# RIGHT
shop-common   <- shared types
shop-domain   -> shop-common
shop-api      -> shop-domain, shop-common

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** five modules each declare their own version of Jackson, and they slowly drift apart.

**Concept:** `<dependencyManagement>` declares versions (and scopes) without adding anything to the classpath; modules then declare the dependency without a version and get the managed one. A BOM (Bill of Materials) is a `pom` that only contains a `dependencyManagement` section, imported with `<type>pom</type>` and `<scope>import</scope>` — Spring Boot, Jackson and Testcontainers publish one.

**How it works:** import a BOM when you cannot use its parent (for example, your company already has its own parent POM).
examples.code:
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <!-- Import a BOM: versions of every Spring Boot-managed library -->
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
      <version>3.4.1</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
    <!-- Your own managed version -->
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.shop</groupId>
      <artifactId>shop-common</artifactId>
      <version>2.1.0</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between dependencyManagement and dependencies?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Declaring a library only in `<dependencyManagement>` and expecting it on the classpath. Management only sets the version; the module still has to list it under `<dependencies>`.
examples.code:
<!-- WRONG: only managed -> "package com.shop.common does not exist" -->
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency><groupId>com.shop</groupId><artifactId>shop-common</artifactId><version>2.1.0</version></dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<!-- RIGHT: also declared (no version needed) -->
<dependencies>
  <dependency><groupId>com.shop</groupId><artifactId>shop-common</artifactId></dependency>
</dependencies>

subsections.subtitle: Plugins and Their Configuration
subsections.description: Configuring what each build step does.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you need code coverage, a minimum Java version check and generated sources — all of it is done by plugins.

**Concept:** everything Maven does is done by plugins, configured in `<build><plugins>`. A plugin has goals; `<executions>` bind goals to lifecycle phases, and `<configuration>` sets parameters. `<pluginManagement>` (usually in a parent) fixes versions and default configuration without activating the plugin; modules then declare it to use it.

**How it works:** `./mvnw help:effective-pom` shows the final configuration after inheritance — the fastest way to understand a confusing build.
examples.code:
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
      <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>0.8.12</version>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals>       <!-- bound to initialize -->
        </execution>
        <execution>
          <id>report</id>
          <phase>verify</phase>
          <goals><goal>report</goal></goals>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

$ ./mvnw help:effective-pom      # the configuration after inheritance
examples.interview_question: How do you attach a plugin goal to a lifecycle phase?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A plugin without a version. Maven picks a default that changes with the Maven version, prints a warning, and the build stops being reproducible. Pin every plugin version (in `pluginManagement`).

subsections.subtitle: Maven Profiles
subsections.description: Conditional build configuration — and when not to use it.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** some build steps should only run sometimes: slow integration tests, a release signing step, a native image.

**Concept:** a profile is a block of configuration that is activated with `-P<id>`, or automatically by a property, the JDK version, the operating system or a file. It can add plugins, dependencies and properties. Use profiles for how the project is built — for example, running slow tests or signing artifacts.

**How it works:** environment-specific values (URLs, passwords) belong in the application's runtime configuration (Spring profiles, environment variables), not in Maven profiles.
examples.interview_question: What are Maven profiles for, and what should not go in them?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: One Maven profile per environment, each producing a different JAR (`-Pdev`, `-Pprod`). The artifact deployed to production is not the one that was tested. Build one artifact and configure it at runtime.
examples.code:
# WRONG: a different build per environment
$ ./mvnw package -Pstaging     # tested
$ ./mvnw package -Pprod        # deployed — never tested

# RIGHT: one JAR, configured when it starts
$ java -jar orders-api.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

subsections.subtitle: Local Repository, Mirrors and settings.xml
subsections.description: Where dependencies come from, and how to authenticate.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the company uses an internal repository (Nexus or Artifactory) that needs a login, and builds fail with "Could not resolve dependencies".

**Concept:** Maven caches every downloaded artifact in the local repository (`~/.m2/repository`), so each version is downloaded once. Remote repositories are Maven Central plus any you declare. `~/.m2/settings.xml` holds per-user settings: credentials for servers (`<servers>`), mirrors that redirect all downloads to an internal proxy (`<mirrors>`), and proxies. A server's `id` must match the repository's `id`.

**How it works:** settings can read environment variables (`${env.NEXUS_TOKEN}`), which is how CI provides credentials.
examples.code:
<!-- ~/.m2/settings.xml -->
<settings>
  <mirrors>
    <mirror>
      <id>company-nexus</id>
      <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>                         <!-- every download goes through Nexus -->
      <url>https://nexus.company.com/repository/maven-public/</url>
    </mirror>
  </mirrors>
  <servers>
    <server>
      <id>company-nexus</id>                         <!-- must match the mirror/repository id -->
      <username>${env.NEXUS_USER}</username>
      <password>${env.NEXUS_TOKEN}</password>
    </server>
  </servers>
</settings>

$ ./mvnw dependency:purge-local-repository -DmanualInclude=com.shop:shop-common   # drop a bad cached copy
examples.interview_question: Where does Maven look for dependencies, and how do you configure credentials for a private repository?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Putting the repository password in the project's `pom.xml`, or committing a `settings.xml` with it. Everyone with access to the code has the credential, forever. Keep credentials in the user's `settings.xml`, reading environment variables.
examples.code:
<!-- WRONG: in pom.xml, committed -->
<repository>
  <id>company-nexus</id>
  <url>https://ci:S3cr3t@nexus.company.com/repository/maven-public/</url>
</repository>

<!-- RIGHT: ~/.m2/settings.xml, from the environment -->
<password>${env.NEXUS_TOKEN}</password>

subsections.subtitle: Speeding Up Builds
subsections.description: Faster feedback locally and in CI.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the build takes eight minutes, so people stop running it before pushing.

**Concept:** build only what changed: `-pl module -am` in multi-module projects. Run modules in parallel with `-T 1C` (one thread per CPU core) when the plugins support it. Skip `clean` when it is not needed — incremental compilation reuses previous output. Run only the relevant tests while developing. In CI, cache `~/.m2` between runs, so dependencies are not downloaded every time.

**How it works:** measure where the time goes before optimizing: often it is one slow test class or one plugin.
examples.code:
$ ./mvnw verify -pl shop-api -am      # only the module you changed (+ what it needs)
$ ./mvnw verify -T 1C                 # modules in parallel, 1 thread per core
$ ./mvnw test -Dtest=OrderServiceTest # only the test you are working on

# GitHub Actions: cache ~/.m2
- uses: actions/setup-java@v4
  with:
    distribution: temurin
    java-version: '21'
    cache: maven
examples.interview_question: How would you make a slow Maven build faster?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A CI pipeline without a dependency cache. Every run downloads hundreds of megabytes from the internet: slow, and it fails whenever the repository has a hiccup.
